extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP office examiners, legal scholars, and students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the U.S. Supreme Court standard (Festo v. Shoketsu) for when claim amendments made during prosecution create prosecution history estoppel that limits application of the doctrine of equivalents, and the circumstances in which a patentee can rebut that presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of claim narrowing on doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrowing amendment during patent prosecution does not necessarily result in a complete bar to the doctrine of equivalents; it raises a rebuttable presumption that the complete bar applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court rejected the Federal Circuit's 'absolute bar' rule and adopted a presumption-of-bar approach: narrowing amendments create a presumption that the patentee surrendered equivalents, but that presumption can be rebutted by the patentee. (See: 'The patentee should bear the burden of showing that the amendment does not surrender the particular equivalent in question.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on patentee to rebut presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee bears the burden of showing that the amendment did not surrender the particular equivalent at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome the presumption, the patentee must demonstrate that, at the time of the amendment, one skilled in the art could not reasonably be expected to have drafted a claim that would have literally encompassed the alleged equivalent. The Court places on the patentee the responsibility to explain why the narrowed claim should still reach the accused equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal factors (exceptions) to prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption that an amendment surrenders equivalents may be rebutted if the patentee proves one of the following: (1) the equivalent was unforeseeable at the time of the amendment; (2) the rationale underlying the amendment bears no more than a tangential relation to the equivalent in question; or (3) there is some other reason suggesting the patentee could not reasonably be expected to have described the alleged equivalent when it narrowed the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three lines of inquiry provide concrete pathways for patentee proof. Courts will evaluate foreseeability of the equivalent, the relation between the amendment's rationale and the specific equivalent, and any other contextual reasons why the patentee could not have been expected to claim the equivalent when narrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original application literally covering the accused device defeats rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the original application once embraced the purported equivalent but the patentee narrowed claims to obtain the patent or to protect validity, the patentee cannot assert that he lacked the words to describe the subject matter in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the original (pre-amendment) claim would have literally covered the accused device, courts will not allow the patentee to rebut the presumption; the rebuttal 'will fail' if the original application literally covered the accused device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — purpose and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents accommodates the difficulty of patent applicants to foresee every possible infringement and allows finding infringement where an accused action, though not literally within the claim, is nevertheless equivalent to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remedial doctrine balances literal claim scope against fair protection; its application must be considered in light of claim amendments and prosecution history so as not to expand claims beyond what was surrendered during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of surrender when claims are narrowed during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder who narrows claims during prosecution is presumed to have surrendered any claim scope (equivalents) that was relinquished by that narrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption creates an evidentiary baseline in infringement litigation: unless rebutted by the patentee under the Festo exceptions, prosecution history estoppel will limit reliance on the doctrine of equivalents for the amended element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common procedural reasons for claim amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are frequently amended during prosecution to respond to rejections under 35 U.S.C. §112 (e.g., failing to disclose how the invention operates), §102 (lack of novelty/anticipation), and §103 (obviousness/lack of inventive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments made to overcome enablement, novelty, or inventive-step objections typically narrow claim scope to distinguish over prior art; such narrowing is the factual basis for applying the presumption of surrender under prosecution history estoppel.
